beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: Sharing an agent isn't one thing, and picking the form is a decision. No cost or risk is attached yet.

beats.trigger: **Bring one example from your own organisation where people got access to a tool and did not use it.**
beats.got: I have this one. The BI licences nobody opened after the acquisition. It's my own material, so I'm paying attention.

beats.trigger: **Test** the switch assumptions and name one person and one test to take out of the room
beats.got: Four verbs, one named person and one test. At least it ends in something I can check.

beats.trigger: What would you want a teammate to have: your `memory/` folder, one of your skills, the morning output, or a way to ask the agent a question in Slack? And why that one?
beats.got: Nothing new. I have no memory folder, no skills, and no Slack agent. This assumes I've built things. 'What would you want' is also close to a feelings question.

beats.trigger: Your agent, skill, output or interface is a candidate for hire: does it do the job better than what they currently use?
beats.got: Judge a tool against what the person does today. That is how I'd judge any spend, so fine. The Christensen citation is noise.

beats.trigger: Does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: The agent reads my files and writes up one controller's job. 'Outcome you could observe' is the first phrase that sounds like a measure.

beats.trigger: If the reason is *"we already have the platform,"* send it back.
beats.got: Don't pick a tool because we already pay for it. That is the sunk-cost trap, and it's what IT always argues. It's the first thing I'd repeat.

beats.trigger: [Design the sharing plan](design-the-sharing-plan.md) finds what would stop that candidate from being absorbed and turns it into a technical plan plus a people plan.
beats.got: Nothing new. It's a pointer to the next exercise.

beats.trigger: Find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: Twenty-three minutes to find one obstacle and write two plans. Reasonable if it produces something I can read.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Find the one constraint behind the others. That is root-cause analysis, so I can use it. It also names trust and governance, which are my objections.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: The tool admits the likely failure is no owner. The unnamed owner is exactly why my three programmes never reached the P&L.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact to `module-7/monday.md`.
beats.got: Nothing new. Another pointer.

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: Calling the plans hypotheses is honest, and less hype than I expected.

beats.trigger: *what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?*
beats.got: List what must be true for them to switch, then test two or three. It's a break-even question in other words. 'Fire their current hire' reads oddly in a Nordic company.

beats.trigger: one person, one question about how they do the job today, and one selected assumption with its test.
beats.got: The output is one named person, one question and one test. That is a small, checkable commitment.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: Pick on outcome, not on fit with the platform. I got that already, so this is a repeat.

beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Access is not absorption
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: Licences issued and people actually using the tool get reported as one figure. I've seen that adoption dashboard, and it is the number I'd stop trusting.

beats.trigger: The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.
beats.got: A good analysis died because leadership's urgency moved. I know that story. There's no cost or payback figure, and fifteen people for two days is a cost nobody mentions. It is at least honest about a failure.

beats.trigger: The fourth does not copy at all, which is why the product being sold as a shared agent is always three of the four parts, with the fourth still sitting with whoever built it.
beats.got: A vendor's shared agent leaves accountability with the builder, so I should ask who answers when it is wrong. That is a due-diligence question I can use.

beats.trigger: Share an interface, and someone has to keep it running and answer for it when it is wrong.
beats.got: Each option has a running cost in someone's time. It names the cost but not the amount.

beats.trigger: Somebody they trust has to have used it first and said so.
beats.got: My controllers will switch from the spreadsheet only if a peer has used the tool and vouched for it. That matches how my team behaves.

beats.trigger: Have the conversation before you build anything more.
beats.got: Talk to one person before spending more. I like that it's cheap, and I could start it this week.

beats.trigger: Who gets your context, who gets a skill, who wants only the output, and who would use an @mention?
beats.got: Nothing new. It's an artifact exercise about who gets what, with no cost or risk in it, and I can't map it onto my team.

beats.trigger: Access is a switch someone flips. Absorption happens in other people's weeks.
beats.got: A recap I'd already got. The last line is the only one I'd keep.

beats.trigger: Their answer is the evidence. The plan is still the hypothesis.
beats.got: The plan is a guess and the conversation is the data. I can hold myself to that.

beats.trigger: ## Next
beats.got: nothing new

take_homes: Rolling out a licence is not the same as people using it, and the two should never be reported as one number.
Before picking a tool or sharing form, ask what job the person does today and what would make them drop what they use now.
Whoever answers for the agent's output is the part that doesn't copy, so I ask who that is before I approve anything.

monday.move: Ask my month-end controller how she writes the variance commentary today, which steps eat the time and who checks it. Build nothing yet.
monday.when: Tuesday, 15 minutes after the weekly finance meeting
monday.stop_condition: If she says the commentary isn't a pain point or she won't use an agent on finance data, I drop it. IT approval is a separate matter.
monday.blocker: IT has not approved any AI tool for finance data, and no one has told me the monthly cost per head.

misconception.why: Licence-versus-capability landed through my own experience with unused tool rollouts. But the module never gave a price or a payback figure, so I still half-think the licence is the main cost.

one_line: Useful if you've already bought the licences and nobody uses them, but it gave me no cost figure, and I'd skip the memory-folder parts.
